senses: A drug mentioned in Homer's Odyssey (c. 8th century B.C.E.) as bringing relief from anxiety or grief; hence, any drug or substance seen as bringing welcome forgetfulness or relief.
ety: Borrowed from Latin nēpenthes (“a drug bringing relief from grief”), from Ancient Greek νηπενθές (nēpenthés), neuter of νηπενθής (nēpenthḗs, “sorrow-banishing”), from νη- (nē-, “not”) + πένθος (pénthos, “grief”) (from πάσχειν (páskhein), present active infinitive of πάσχω (páskhō, “to be ill or injured in a certain way; to suffer”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷendʰ- (“to endure, to suffer”)). Compare French népenthès (“a plant from which a drug supposedly bringing relief from grief may be obtained; such a drug”).
examples: The nepenth of nostalgia is replaced by an amphetamine of anticipation.

senses: A small two-masted, and later three-masted, Mediterranean transport ship with an overhanging bow and stern.
ety: From French chebec, from Spanish xabeque or Catalan xabec or Italian sciabecco, from Arabic شُبَّاك (šubbāk, “fishing-net”). Not to confuse with the sambuq, an Indian-Sea vessel.
examples: Winter. The green xebec whose figurehead was Astarte, goddess of sexual love, tacked slowly into the Grand Harbour.

senses: Study of cryptids, animals whose existence has not been proven.
ety: From crypto- + zoology.
examples: The Loch Ness Monster is one of the mysteries of cryptozoology.

senses: The edible tuber of Conopodium majus, native to western Europe.
Simmondsia chinensis, jojoba.
Pelleted food for pigs.
ety: From pig + nut.
examples: Justus partially overcame their scruples against work, and taught them that the black earth was rich in other produce than pignuts only.

senses: A small spark or flash.
A small or trace amount.
ety: Existing in English since the 17th century; borrowed from Latin scintilla (“spark”).
examples: If the action of the electrodynamic waves is so violent that, even without artificial electrification of the secondary conductor, scintillæ occur in its spark-gap, the aluminium leaves remain almost without change.

Current medical practice recommends use of heroic measures if there is a scintilla of a chance that the patient will recover, on the assumption that the measures will be discontinued should the patient improve.

It’s 3pm at Rizes, a farm in the heart of Mykonos, and there is not a champagne bottle in sight, a sunbed to lounge on, or a scintilla of music that might drown the sound of the winds breezing through the nearby bamboo.

senses: A product produced and sold independently of corporations (in Japan); an indie work.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 同人 (dōjin, “colleague, people with similar interests”, literally “same people”). The spelling is derived from the informal wāpuro rōmaji romanization style of 同人 (どうじん, do-u-ji-n).
examples: Thus, roughly a third of all circles in Comic Market participate for the purpose of creating doujin without the goal of transitioning to commercial publications.
There are creators who really make money and earn living from doujin, but those who can do so, are minority.

senses: Showing contempt; expressing disdain; showing a lack of respect.
ety: From Latin contemptus (whence contempt) + -ous.
examples: I don't know that guy, but he just gave me a contemptuous look.
Sir George burst into a loud fit of contemptuous laughter.

senses: Synonym of spooky.
Involving horror concepts and tropes in comical, cute, or nonthreatening ways.
ety: A misspelling of spooky, originating from a 2009 photograph of a Halloween sign with the misspelled word spoopy originally uploaded to the website Flickr. It was reposted on Tumblr in 2011, upon which the word become an Internet meme and developed its current senses.
examples: Hey Alan, did you know when Romance wears those black jackets he looks spoopier?
To get into the spoopy spirit, you will exclusively listen to the "Spooky Scary Skeletons" trap remix on repeat from now until Halloween.
It's spoopy season – a time for pumpkin carving, trick or treating and "Hocus Pocus" reruns.

senses: Smoldering; slow combustion.
Cookware used in such cooking.
The state of being stifled; suppression.
Stifling smoke; thick dust.
The act of smothering a kick (see verb section).
ety: From Middle English smother, smorther (“a suffocating vapour, dense smoke”), from Old English smorþor (“smoke”, literally “that which suffocates”), from smorian (“to suffocate, choke”) + -þor (instrumental suffix).
examples: Thus must I from the smoke into the smother, / From tyrant duke unto tyrant brother.

senses: High-pitched and piercing.
Having a shrill voice.
Sharp or keen to the senses.
ety: From Late Middle English schrille, shirle, shrille (“of a sound: high-pitched, piercing; producing such a sound”), possibly from the earlier shil, schille (“loud, resounding; high-pitched”), from Old English sċill (“sonorous sounding”), of Germanic origin and probably ultimately imitative. The r in the word was introduced by analogy to Middle English skrīke, skrīken, scrēmen, possibly to avoid confusion with non-Anglian forms of schelle (modern English shell) where Old English sċill (“sonorous sounding”) and sċill (“shell”) existed. The word is cognate with Icelandic skella (“crash, bang, slam
examples: The woods rang with shrill cries of the birds.

But I discovered no trace of him, and was beginning to conjecture that some fortunate chance had intervened to prevent the execution of his menaces; when suddenly I heard a shrill and dreadful scream.

senses: Angular, bony, and lean.
Unhealthily thin, as from hunger or illness: drawn, emaciated, haggard.
Of a place or thing: bleak, desolate.
ety: From Middle English gaunt, gawnt, gawnte, gant (“lean, slender, thin, gaunt”); further etymology uncertain. Speculated origins include: * from a North Germanic/Scandinavian source related to Old Norse gandr (“magic staff; stick”) (the ancestor of Icelandic gandur (“magic staff”) and Norwegian gand (“thin, pointed stick; tall, thin man”)), from Proto-Germanic *gandaz (“stick; staff”). Other suggested Germanic cognates include Swedish gank (“(dialectal) lean, emaciated horse”); Danish gand, gan, Norwegian gana (“cut-off tree limbs”); Bavarian Gunten (“kind of peg or wedge”). These words have all
examples: Hanging from the beam, / Slowly swaying (such the law), / Gaunt the shadow on your green, / Shenandoah!
He rose with difficulty; a tall, gaunt, terrible form, black and weird against the shining sea and the starry skies.
The leafless trees were surging in the night-wind; their gaunt branches were waving grimly over her head.

senses: To evade or escape from (someone or something), especially by using cunning or skill.
To shake off (a pursuer); to give someone the slip.
To escape being understandable to; to be incomprehensible to.
To escape someone's memory, to slip someone's mind.
ety: From Latin ēlūdō (“to evade, elude”), from ē- (“out of”, short form of ex-) + lūdō (“to play; to trick”).
examples: Thus the observation of human blindness and weakness is the result of all philosophy, and meets us at every turn, in spite of our endeavours to elude or avoid it.
The line continued in operation until about 1908, but the precise date of closure has eluded research.
It leaves City still searching for the Champions League, the trophy that has always eluded them

senses: An object inserted to hold a space open in a row of items, e.g. beads or printed type.
A person who works or lives in space.
An instrument for reversing a telegraphic current, especially in a marine cable, to increase the speed of transmission.
ety: From space + -er.
examples: The vertical wall was poured in two lifts, using two pairs of steel shutters which were bolted tightly onto 9-in. long wooden spacers.
It was the futile throwing back in the face of the Spacers their most keenly felt insult: their insistence on considering the natives of Earth as disgustingly diseased.
He was thankful that he still had his suit on when the ship had a catastrophic decompression, a spacer's worst nightmare.

senses: To become cozy; (by extension) to become acquainted, comfortable, or familiar with.
ety: From coz(y) + -en.
examples: A wasp nest cozened up in the corner of the far ceiling.
I heard someone at the swap meet say they were going to cozen up to someone, and someone else told me my sales pitch was a filibuster.

senses: A design or piece of art which is engraved or etched into something.
Any printing method in which the ink is laid upon the sunken parts of the printing form.
ety: Borrowed from Italian intaglio, from intagliare (“to engrave”).
examples: On a wooden pub sign daringly taken, one daylight raid, by a drunken Bartley Gobbitch, across which still survives in intaglio the legend SNIPE AND SHAFT, Teddy Bloat is mincing bananas with a great isosceles knife.

senses: A hairstyle.
ety: From hair + do.
examples: Halogen light glares off the man's slick hairdo.
Jennifer Garner is a star of many talents and now many hairdos.
Between an asymmetrical bob and pixie cut, Houston paired her short hairdo with a glazed red lip, tonal purple eyeshadow, and chocolate blush.

senses: Any of certain wild canids of the genera Lupulella and Canis, native to the tropical Old World and smaller than a wolf.
A person who performs menial or routine tasks; a dogsbody.
ety: Borrowed from French chacal, chacale, checale, schakal, ciacale, from Turkish çakal, from Ottoman Turkish چقال (çakâl), from Classical Persian شغال (šaġāl), borrowed from Sanskrit शृगाल (śṛgāla, “jackal”), the alternative form of सृगाल (sṛgāla).
examples: Until recently, scientists thought Ethiopian wolves were a type of jackal. They gave Ethiopian wolves names like Semien jackal, Simenian jackal, or Ethiopian jackal.
As we will see, the jackal is usually associated in the Indic context with death and impurity, and would therefore sit squarely at the bottom of Dumont's social hierarchy.

A nephew of hers, after receiving some learning at her ladyship's expence, got a commission, and fell upon the field of Waterloo; another is still at her heels, as a sort of jackall to fetch and carry when required.

senses: A confection consisting of a nut, seed or fruit coated with sugar.
ety: From Old French confit (“preserved fruit”), from Latin cōnfectum. Doublet of confect, confetto, confit, and konfyt. Compare confit.
examples: Heart! you swear like a comfit-maker's wife.
But since I ate your present of comfits—and they were admirable comfits, and I ate them with speed—my heart is changed and inclined toward you, I know not why or how, except it be through magic.

senses: A type of electronic percussion device.
ety: From beat + box.
examples: Self-styled 'black gentleman vampire' who followed his cousin in to hip-hop by rapping in front of a beatbox for his first shows on Long Island, New York.
But by 1980 Fenley had collaborated with Mark Freedman on the high-energy, repetitive sound score for Energizer by manipulating a beatbox, the omnipresent instrument of late disco music.
Hip-hop took the language and made it graffiti—it was music video on a wall with a beatbox blowing its subwoofers next to it.

senses: A shuttle bus in France.
A kind of grape that grows in summer.
A lenticular piece of jewelry.
ety: From French navette. By surface analysis, Latin nav- + -ette.
examples: To address this, we explore the case of the navettes, informal vans that operate in the unlikely and unfriendly formal transport landscape of Brussels.
The summer Navette is less cultivated than the Coleseed, being less prolific, the seeds being much smaller.

senses: Any of a number of wild flowering plants with yellow flowers in the family Asteraceae, mostly belonging to Senecio and related genera.
ety: From rag (referring to the ragged leaves) + wort.
examples: Ragwort is under the command of dame Venus, and cleanses, digests and discusses.
Sea-poppies and ragwort were plants of ill-fame, too.

senses: Any bacilliform (rod-shaped) bacterium.
Something which spreads like bacterial infection.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin bacillus (“little staff, wand”), diminutive of baculum (“stick, staff, walking stick”).
examples: The “bacillus of boom or depression,” he wrote, travels freely “from country to country.”

senses: To detect (a flavour or taste, or food or drink); to taste; specifically, to enjoy or linger on (a flavour or taste, or food and drink); to relish.
To give (food or drink) flavour; to flavour, to season.
To enjoy (something) deeply or in a lingering manner; to appreciate, to delight in, to relish.
To find (something) appealing; to appreciate, to like.
To possess a particular (often negative) quality, especially a small amount of it; to be redolent or suggestive of.
ety: From Middle English savouren, savour, from Anglo-Norman savorer, savourer, Middle French savorer, savourer, and Old French savorer, savourer (modern French savourer), from Late Latin sapōrāre, the present active infinitive of sapōrō (“to give flavour, make tasty; to give pleasure”), from Latin sapor (see etymology 1) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs).
examples: He closed his eyes so he could really savour his dessert.
What Flesh is fitting for Man to Eat, / Until our Herbs do savour the Meat?
A journey along the Conwy Valley line is one to savour for aficionados of scenic railways.

senses: A composition for nine instruments or nine voices.
ety: From Italian nonetto, from nono (“ninth”).
examples: The small-group sides are the best, with the nonet in particular coming through as a sparkling unit that deserves an LP to itself.

senses: Much; a great deal of.
ety: From Spanish mucho. Unrelated to much.
examples: Seemed like the real thing, only to find / Mucho mistrust, love's gone behind
There will be calamities, maudlin melodramas, and mucho pathos at Cries & Whispers--A Tragedy Club, which seeks to reverse our town's love of comedy.

senses: An extension or projection from something.
ety: From pseudo- + -pod.
examples: A pseudopod of blackness elongated itself from the central mass and like a great tentacle clutched the corpse-like being, dragged it back to the pit and over the brink.

senses: A Maori dirge, or song for the dead.
Funeral rites; a funeral ceremony, a tangihanga.
Crying, wailing, especially when seeing someone after a long absence.
ety: Borrowed from Māori tangi (“lament, mourning, funeral ceremony”).
examples: Late in the nineteenth century Māori women began to adopt the Victorian mourning costume of black clothes for tangi, and the practice continued long after Pākehā New Zealanders had dropped the custom.

senses: (obsolete) To fuck.
ety: Coined by Richard Francis Burton from French foutre, from Latin futuo, futuere.
examples: When Doge is not feeding or futtering, depend on it, he is hunting.
And they began disputing about futtering her.

senses: somewhat sweet (all senses)
ety: From sweet + -ish.
examples: At the church sociables he used to hop around among them, chipping and chirping like a dicky-bird picking up seed; and he was a great hand to play the piano, and sing saddish, sweetish songs to them.
Up half the night, nearly 'til dawn, I can almost see the light in a love that can't go wrong, It's just another sweetish love song.
Pine Nuts are sweetish in flavor, warming, and lack poison.

senses: A diocese: a region in which a bishop of a church governs.
The office or function of a bishop.
ety: From Middle English bischopriche, from Old English bisċoprīċe, equivalent to bishop + -ric (compare German Reich).
examples: Later that year, he was appointed to the bishopric of Lindesmeere.
Wiltshire actually comes from Wiltonshire, for Wilton was once a county town, royal residence and bishopric - a place of significance.

senses: Something that speeds up a process or the uptake of something else.
ety: From accelerate + -ant (suffix forming agent nouns from verbs, or forming adjectives with senses of being prone or tending to do the actions of verbs).
examples: Hello Neighbor’s experience reflects the rise of video sites like YouTube as an accelerant for the video game business.

senses: The quality of being inclusive; inclusiveness.
ety: From inclusive + -ity, modeled after exclusivity, 1920s, but in more common usage only since the late 1980s.
examples: Modern states have ordered and arranged their racial inclusivities on the necessity of racist exclusivities.
These are the terms on which Gandhi gives birth to Hindu inclusivity. It is worth pausing to distinguish Hindu inclusivity from Christian inclusivity.
Within a single organization scheme, you will need to balance the tension between exclusivity and inclusivity.

senses: Of an event, situation, etc.: to appear or happen again, especially repeatedly.
Of a memory, thought, etc.: to come to the mind again.
To speak, think, or write about something again; to go back or return to a memory, a subject, etc.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin recurrō (“to hurry or run back; to return, revert”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘back, backwards’) + currō (“to hasten, hurry; to move, travel; to run”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”)). cognates * Anglo-Norman recurre, recorre (“to have recourse to”) * Catalan recórrer * Italian ricorrer * Old French recourir (Middle French recourir; modern French recourir (“to have recourse to; to run again; to run back”)) * Old Occitan recorre * Portuguese recorrer * Spanish recorrer
examples: The theme of the prodigal son recurs later in the third act.
All this pressed on his mind; yet the original statement recurred with the same irresistible force.
But the knot of causes recurreth in which I am twined. It will create me again! I myself belong unto the causes of eternal recurrence.

senses: Love and compassion.
ety: From Māori aroha. Doublet of aloha and aropa.
examples: As much as possible, even under threat, mana should be tempered with aroha.
They do not come to this meeting house with respect, nor with aroha.
I am filled with aroha and compassion for our Muslim communities, for all migrants, for refugees and for Christchurch.

senses: Defeated, overcome.
ety: Participle adjective of the verb worst.
examples: The worsted army fled in disarray.

senses: The craft of making statues.
Statues considered collectively.
ety: From Latin statuāria (ars) (“(art) of sculpture”), feminine of the adjective statuārius (“of statues”).
examples: Simply on aesthetic grounds I can almost applaud the Victorians’ fig obsessed Bowdlerisation of Greek and Roman statuary.

senses: Overly, affectedly or unnecessarily cute; too cute to be taken seriously.
ety: From cute + -sy.
examples: The couple called each other cutesy pet names like "honeypot" and "smoochie-poochie" that disgusted everyone else.
If each subject attracts roughly the same amount of attention (and with a judgmental adjustment to drop the more cutesy papers), that's roughly 100 papers per topic.

senses: A fictional alien creature in Star Trek, a fast-breeding, cooing ball of fur.
ety: Probably invented for alliteration with trouble; the creatures first appeared in an episode called "The Trouble with Tribbles".
examples: The Hyper-Producing Playwrights of Edmondton: Or Why Alberta’s Capital Breeds New Plays Like Tribbles.
They were like tribbles, multiplying by the dozens, cackling, giggling their maniacal joy at the game.
They breed like tribbles, but at least they’re not terrestrial.

senses: A German- or Austrian-style sausage.
ety: First attested in 1890. Borrowed from German Wurst (“sausage, wurst”), from Middle High German wurst, from Old High German wurst, from Proto-West Germanic *wursti (“something turned or twisted”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert-, *werd- (“to turn”). Akin to Old Saxon worst (“wurst”), Old English weorþan (“to turn, become”). Doublet of wors. Unrelated to worsted (“type of yarn”). More at worth (“to be, become, betide”).
examples: We had a long walk ahead to Stuttgart. We stopped to eat at a little meat market just outside Augsburg. I bought a loaf of bread and chose a couple of packages of wurst. It really was good.
Although the supermarket tannoy was bravely broadcasting Rigoletto, its meat counter was thick with wurst and its wine shelves loaded with Liebfraumilch.
At an open-air flea market, we looked for Nazi memorabilia while munching wurst and drinking beer.

senses: Conceited and overconfident of knowledge but poorly informed and immature.
Pretentious; inflated in style or manner.
ety: From sophomore + -ic.
examples: The editors agree with that “and make that puerile, sophomoric, and jejune too,” says Beard.
